ios.desc:
Jotcal is a family calendar designed to be seen, not managed.

A single calm surface that shows what's happening today, without making you tap, scroll, or search. Put it on a tablet on the kitchen wall, or keep it in your pocket. It reads the same way.

WRITE IT BY HAND
Jot an event with Apple Pencil. Handwriting recognition turns your note into a calendar entry. No forms, no dropdowns.

FIVE WAYS TO READ YOUR DAY
Agenda, Grid, Timeline, Daybook, and the Dial. Pick the one that fits how you think, or the one that reads best from across the room.

BUILT FOR THE WALL
On a tablet, Jotcal becomes an ambient display: large, quiet, legible at a distance.

WEATHER ON THE DAY
Sunrise, daylight, and rain sit on the day itself, not in a separate tab you never open.

WORKS WITH WHAT YOU ALREADY USE
Your existing calendars, on your device. No new account, no sign-up, no lock-in.

PRIVACY
No account. No analytics. We don't measure how you use the app. No ads. Your handwriting never leaves your device. Jotcal contains no third-party SDKs of any kind.

PAY ONCE
One payment, yours forever. No subscription. Handwriting and calendar sync are always free. Pro unlocks every view, weather on your days, and the widgets. Buy once and every future update is included at today's price.

quotes.text:
Jotcal started almost two decades ago as an idea for a wall calendar that combined the best of the paper calendars and whiteboards I grew up with and the cloud calendars I carry everywhere now. I wanted the calm, there-at-a-glance visibility and the tactility and speed of a handwritten scribble over form fields and on-screen keyboards, but I still wanted it on all of my devices, shared with my family and updated in real time.

When I started designing it I had to think about why I wanted those things, what I was trying to achieve with the visibility, the convenience of data entry and the integration with the rest of my life, and I realised it was a chance to rethink the whole experience around some core principles. Everything on the calendar should earn its place, ideally by being actionable, important information should be prominent, and when there's nothing important or imminent it should be calm and not fight for attention.

It's a one-time purchase, no subscription, with a 14-day trial of everything before the app drops back to a simpler free calendar (handwriting and calendar sync stay free). I've kept the tracking as light as I could, which means no analytics and your calendar goes directly between your device and your own accounts. Both platforms record a small amount of data on a server for tracking the trial and Android sends crash reports, which are on by default and can be switched off in Settings. The privacy policy lists exactly what leaves your device.
